why.correct: The diaphysis is the shaft: the long middle part of the bone between the two flared ends.
options: An epiphysis is one of the widened ends of the bone, not the long middle part.
Correct. The long shaft is the diaphysis.
A metaphysis is the short flared zone where the shaft widens into an end. The pinned region runs most of the bone's length.
The medullary cavity is the hollow inside the shaft. The pinned region is the whole shaft, wall and all.

why.correct: The medullary cavity is the hollow inside the diaphysis. In an adult it is filled with yellow marrow.
options: Correct. The hollow center of the shaft is the medullary cavity.
A nutrient foramen is a small hole through the shaft wall for the nutrient artery, not the long central space.
The proximal epiphysis is the widened upper end of the bone, not a space inside the shaft.
The endosteum is the thin cell layer lining the cavity, not the cavity itself.

why.correct: The periosteum is the membrane covering the outer surface of the bone. Its fibrous layer anchors tendons and ligaments, and it is rich in nerves and vessels.
options: The endosteum lines the inside of the bone, facing the medullary cavity, not its outer surface.
Articular cartilage covers only the joint surfaces at the ends, and it is cartilage, not a membrane over the shaft.
Correct. The outer membrane of a bone is the periosteum.
The perichondrium wraps cartilage, not bone. The shaft of an adult long bone is covered by periosteum.

why.correct: Yellow bone marrow fills the medullary cavity of an adult's long bones. It is mostly adipose tissue.
options: Red marrow in an adult long bone sits in the lattice of the ends, not in the middle of the shaft's cavity.
Articular cartilage caps the joint surfaces at the ends of the bone, not the inside of the shaft.
The endosteum is a thin lining of cells, not the tissue filling the cavity.
Correct. The fatty tissue in the shaft's cavity is yellow bone marrow.

why.correct: The nutrient artery is the main artery of a long bone. It enters the diaphysis through a nutrient foramen and branches along the medullary cavity.
options: Correct. The artery entering the middle of the shaft is the nutrient artery.
A nutrient vein does leave through the same hole, but the drawn vessel is red and carries blood into the bone: it is the artery.
The periosteum is the membrane over the bone's surface, not a vessel.
Articular cartilage caps the joint surfaces at the ends of the bone; it is not a vessel.

why.correct: A tuberosity is a large, rough, raised area where a tendon attaches. This one is where a shoulder muscle pulls on the upper arm bone.
options: An epicondyle is a bump on or above a condyle, at the end of a bone, not a rough area partway along the shaft.
Correct. A rough raised area for a tendon is a tuberosity.
A fossa is a shallow depression, not a raised area.
A facet is a small, flat, smooth joint surface, not a rough attachment area.

why.correct: A crest is a long, prominent ridge. This is the curved top edge of the hip bone, which you can feel at your waist.
options: A spine is a sharp, slender, pointed process, not a long curved ridge.
A fossa is a shallow basin. On this figure the fossa lies just below the ridge, on the inner face of the bone.
Correct. The long curved ridge is a crest.
A head is a rounded end set on a neck that forms a joint, not a ridge along a bone's edge.

why.correct: Bones are classified by shape, not size. A bone that is longer than it is wide, with a shaft and two ends, is a long bone, however small.
options: Short bones are about as wide as they are long, like the cube-shaped bones of the wrist. A finger bone has a clear shaft.
A sesamoid bone is a small round bone that forms inside a tendon. A finger bone forms a normal part of the finger's frame and has a shaft.
Irregular bones have complex shapes that fit no other group. A shaft with two ends is the long-bone pattern.
Correct. Shape, not size, makes it a long bone.

why.correct: A sesamoid bone (sesam- = sesame seed) is a small, round bone that develops inside a tendon where it crosses a joint. The bone at the front of the knee is the largest.
options: That describes a flat bone, such as the breastbone or a rib.
That describes short bones, such as those of the wrist and ankle.
Correct. Sesamoid bones sit inside tendons.
That describes an irregular bone, such as a vertebra.

why.correct: Through childhood, fat cells replace the red marrow in the shafts of the limb bones. In an adult, red marrow remains mainly in the flat bones, vertebrae and hip bones, and in the upper ends of the thigh and upper arm bones. The shaft's cavity holds yellow marrow, which makes no blood cells.
options: Correct. An adult's long-bone shafts hold yellow marrow; the hip bone still holds red marrow.
The hip bone is covered by periosteum like every other bone surface that is not a joint surface. The site is chosen for its marrow, not its covering.
Newborns have red marrow in almost every bone. It is in adults that red marrow retreats to the flat bones, vertebrae, hip bones and the upper ends of two long bones.
The shaft of a long bone is a hollow tube: its medullary cavity is filled with yellow marrow in an adult.

why.correct: The periosteum covers the outer surface of the bone and is packed with sensory nerve endings. On the shin, a blow crushes it between the skin and the bone.
options: Yellow marrow lies deep inside the shaft and is mostly fat. A blow to the surface does not reach it first.
Correct. The periosteum is richly supplied with nerves and lies right under the skin on the shin.
Articular cartilage covers joint surfaces at the ends of the bone, not the middle of the shin. It has no nerves at all.
The endosteum lines the inside of the bone and has fewer nerves. The periosteum takes the blow.

why.correct: The skeleton supports the body, protects organs, allows movement, stores minerals (about 99% of the body's calcium), makes blood cells in red marrow, and stores fat in yellow marrow.
options: Correct. Bone is the body's mineral bank.
Correct. Red marrow carries out hematopoiesis.
Vitamin D is made in the skin, from a cholesterol derivative, when ultraviolet light strikes it. Bone uses calcium, but it does not make the vitamin.
Correct. The skull, vertebrae and rib cage enclose the brain, spinal cord, heart and lungs.
Correct. Yellow marrow is mostly adipose tissue that stores triglycerides.
Filtering waste from the blood is done by the kidneys, not by bone.

why.correct: The periosteum's outer fibrous layer comes first, then its inner cellular layer, which lies against the bone. Next is the thick wall of dense bone, then the endosteum lining the inside of that wall, and finally the medullary cavity, filled with yellow marrow in an adult.
The metaphysis (meta- = between) is the flared region where the shaft widens into the end of the bone.
options: The medullary cavity is inside the shaft, not a region between the shaft and the end.
Correct. The metaphysis lies between diaphysis and epiphysis.
The periosteum covers the outside of the whole bone. It is not a region along its length.
Articular cartilage caps the epiphysis at the joint, beyond it rather than before it.

why.correct: The periosteum covers the bone everywhere except where articular cartilage covers it. The joint surfaces are bare cartilage, which is what lets two bones glide on each other.
options: This statement is right. Periosteum covers the outer surface of the shaft.
This statement is right. Tendon collagen blends into the fibrous layer, so a muscle's pull passes into the bone.
This is the error. The periosteum stops at the edge of the articular cartilage; the joint surface itself has no periosteum.
This statement is right. Articular cartilage is hyaline cartilage.
This statement is right. Articular cartilage has no blood vessels; it gets its nutrients from the fluid in the joint.

why.correct: A condyle is a smooth, rounded knob that meets another bone at a joint, like the two knobs at the lower end of the thigh bone that form the knee.
options: A crest is a long ridge where muscles attach, not a joint surface.
A tuberosity is a rough raised area where a tendon attaches.
A trochanter is a very large process on the thigh bone where muscles attach.
Correct. Condyles, heads and facets are the joint-forming markings.

why.correct: Tuberosities and crests are where tendons pull. Where muscles pull hard and often for years, the bone under the tendon grows more raised and rough. Heavy, repeated muscle use is the likely difference.
options: Correct. The shape of a marking follows the pull on it.
Red marrow sits inside the bone and does not shape surface markings.
Rougher attachment sites reflect how hard muscles pulled on the bone, not the age growth stopped.
Articular cartilage covers joint surfaces; tuberosities and crests are attachment sites away from the joints.

why.correct: Yellow marrow keeps the ability to become red marrow. When the demand for blood cells stays high, stem cells repopulate it and it starts making blood cells again.
options: Articular cartilage covers the joint surfaces and does not contain marrow; it is not converted.
Red marrow turning yellow is the normal change through childhood. It would reduce blood cell formation, not raise it.
Correct. Yellow marrow can revert to red when more blood cells are needed.
The periosteum holds bone-building cells and stem cells for bone, but it does not make blood cells.

why.correct: The nutrient foramen is a small slanting hole through the shaft wall. The nutrient artery enters through it and the nutrient vein leaves, and nerves travel with them.
options: Tendons attach to the periosteum and bone surface. They do not pass through holes into the cavity.
Marrow stays inside the bone. The hole carries vessels.
Correct. The nutrient foramen carries the bone's main vessels.
The periosteum covers the outer surface; the inner surfaces are lined by endosteum.

why.correct: Red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets all come from stem cells in red marrow. Damage the stem cells and, as old cells die off, all three fall; the shortest-lived fall first.
options: White blood cells do fall, but they are not the only product of the marrow's stem cells.
Red blood cells do fall, but more slowly, and the other lines fall too.
Correct. Hematopoiesis makes all three from the same stem cells.
Platelets fall, but so do the other cells made from the same stem cells.

why.correct: The osteoclast is a very large cell with several nuclei and a frilled membrane pressed against the bone. It resorbs bone.
options: Osteoblasts are medium-sized cells with one nucleus that sit in rows on bone surfaces.
An osteocyte is a small cell with long branching arms, inside the matrix.
An osteogenic cell is a flat stem cell with one nucleus.
Correct. Huge, many nuclei, frilled edge on the bone: an osteoclast.

why.correct: Osteoblasts line up on bone surfaces and secrete osteoid, the organic matrix that later mineralizes.
options: Osteocytes sit alone inside the matrix, each in a lacuna, not in a row on the surface.
Correct. A row of bone-building cells on the surface is a row of osteoblasts.
Osteoclasts are single huge cells with many nuclei, not a row of ordinary-sized cells.
Chondrocytes are cartilage cells in lacunae within cartilage matrix, not bone-surface cells.

why.correct: The osteogenic cell is the stem cell of bone. It lies in the periosteum and endosteum, it is the only bone cell that divides, and its daughters become osteoblasts.
options: Correct. The dividing stem cell of bone is the osteogenic cell.
Osteoblasts are made from this cell, and they do not divide.
Mesenchymal cells are the embryonic cells that connective tissues come from. The pinned cell sits on a finished bone surface, as the stem cell of bone.
Osteoclasts come from a different line, related to macrophages, and they are huge, not flat.

why.correct: Trabeculae are the thin struts of spongy bone, with marrow in the spaces between them.
options: Osteons are the cylinders of compact bone, each with a central canal. The struts of spongy bone have none.
Central canals are channels down the middle of osteons in compact bone. Spongy bone has none, and the pinned structures are solid struts.
Correct. The branching struts are trabeculae.
Canaliculi are hair-thin channels within the matrix, far smaller than the struts.

why.correct: A lacuna is a small cavity between lamellae. Each one holds a single osteocyte.
options: A central canal runs down the middle of an osteon and carries vessels. Spongy bone has none.
Correct. The small pit that holds an osteocyte is a lacuna.
A perforating canal is a channel running across compact bone between osteons, not a small cell-sized pit.
A canaliculus is a hair-thin channel running from a lacuna, not the cavity itself.

why.correct: Canaliculi are hair-thin channels that radiate from each lacuna. The arms of osteocytes run through them, linking the cells to each other and to a supply of blood.
options: Correct. The fine radiating channels are canaliculi.
Lacunae are the small cavities the channels connect, not the channels themselves.
Perforating canals are much larger channels in compact bone that carry vessels between osteons.
Collagen fibers are part of the matrix and are not visible as open channels.

why.correct: Vinegar is an acid, and acid dissolves the calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite) crystals, just as the acid from osteoclasts does. What remains is the collagen framework, which is flexible but cannot resist squeezing.
options: If the collagen and ground substance had gone, the bone would be hard and brittle, as it is after baking. The bone bends because they remain.
Removing cells would not change how hard or flexible the matrix is; the matrix sets those properties.
Correct. The acid dissolved the mineral and left the flexible collagen.
The periosteum is a thin outer membrane. Its loss would not make the whole bone rubbery.

why.correct: Collagen resists pulling and gives bone slight flexibility. Mineral without good collagen is like chalk: hard but brittle, so it snaps instead of bending. This inherited condition is called brittle bone disease.
options: The question says her bone is fully mineralized, so storing mineral is not the problem.
Correct. Faulty collagen leaves hard but brittle bone.
Osteoclasts are not affected by a collagen defect, and failing to resorb bone would not in itself make bones snap.
Lacunae hold osteocytes. A collagen defect does not remove them, and it is the matrix that sets strength.

why.correct: Osteogenic cells are the stem cells of bone. They divide, and their daughters differentiate into osteoblasts.
options: Osteoblasts are made by osteogenic cells and do not divide.
Osteocytes are former osteoblasts trapped in matrix; they do not divide.
Osteoclasts form by fusion of precursor cells, not by division, and do not divide.
Correct. Only the osteogenic cell divides.

why.correct: Osteoclasts form when several precursor cells from the blood-forming line in red marrow, the line that also makes macrophages, fuse. That is why they have several nuclei. They are not part of the osteogenic cell to osteoblast to osteocyte line.
options: Osteoblasts become osteocytes, not osteoclasts. The two cell types come from different lines.
Correct. Osteoclasts are fused cells of the macrophage line.
Osteocytes stay in their lacunae for life. They do not become osteoclasts.
Osteogenic cells make osteoblasts. Osteoclasts come from a separate, blood-forming line.

why.correct: Osteogenic cells divide and their daughters become osteoblasts. An osteoblast secretes osteoid, which then mineralizes. As matrix builds up around it, the cell ends up enclosed in a lacuna. It is now an osteocyte, still linked to its neighbors by arms running through canaliculi.
Mineralized matrix is almost impermeable. Osteocytes get oxygen and nutrients only from vessels in the central canal, passed along through canaliculi. Block the canaliculi and the cells starve.
options: They cannot carry on normally: nutrients cannot diffuse through mineralized matrix, which is why canaliculi exist.
Osteocytes do not divide.
Osteocytes do not become osteoclasts; the two come from different cell lines.
Correct. The canaliculi are their only supply line.

why.correct: Spongy bone is a lattice of trabeculae with marrow in the spaces between them. It fills the ends of long bones and the inside of other bones, and its osteocytes sit in lacunae like those of compact bone.
options: Correct. Trabeculae are its struts.
Osteons with central canals are the units of compact bone. Trabeculae are thin enough not to need a central canal.
Correct. Its spaces hold marrow, red in some bones.
Correct. The epiphyses are filled with spongy bone.
About 80% of the skeleton's mass is compact bone. Spongy bone is about 20%.
Correct. Osteocytes of spongy bone also live in lacunae, linked by canaliculi.

why.correct: Osteogenic cells become osteoblasts, and osteoblasts walled in by their own matrix become osteocytes.
options: Osteoclasts come from a different line, related to macrophages, and do not become osteocytes.
Chondrocytes are cartilage cells, not a stage between bone stem cells and osteocytes.
Correct. The osteoblast is the middle stage.
Fibroblasts make connective tissue fibers and are not part of the bone cell line.

why.correct: The calcium and phosphate freed from the matrix move into the blood. That is how bone works as a mineral bank: osteoclasts withdraw minerals from it.
options: This step is right. The sealed space keeps the acid and enzymes against the bone.
This step is right. Pumped hydrogen ions acidify the sealed space.
This step is right. Acid dissolves hydroxyapatite.
This step is right. Once the mineral is gone, lysosomal enzymes digest the exposed collagen.
This is the error. The released minerals pass into the blood rather than being stored in the cell.

why.correct: In the flat bones of the skull, a layer of spongy bone is sandwiched between two plates of compact bone. That spongy layer is the diploë.
options: Correct. Diploë is the name for spongy bone in flat skull bones.
The outer shell is compact bone; the diploë is the spongy layer inside it.
The lining of the medullary cavity is the endosteum.
The central canal is the vessel channel of an osteon, found in compact bone.

why.correct: Perforating canals run across compact bone, crosswise to the osteons. They carry vessels between central canals and out to the periosteum and marrow.
options: Canaliculi are tiny channels that link lacunae to each other and to the central canal within one osteon. They are too small to carry blood vessels.
Central canals run along the length of each osteon. The channels asked about run across the bone, joining those central canals.
Correct. Perforating canals connect the central canals crosswise.
Trabeculae are the struts of spongy bone, not channels in compact bone.

why.correct: Like the crossed layers of plywood, fibers that spiral in opposite directions in neighboring lamellae resist twisting from either direction.
options: Acid dissolves mineral whatever direction the collagen runs.
Correct. Alternating fiber directions resist twisting.
Vessels run in the central and perforating canals; fiber direction does not block them.
Mineral deposits along the collagen fibers in every lamella; their direction does not prevent it.

why.correct: Osteoblasts and osteoclasts work on bone surfaces. The thin trabeculae of spongy bone expose far more surface per gram than compact bone does, so a shift toward breakdown removes spongy bone faster.
options: Spongy bone has osteocytes in lacunae, just as compact bone does.
Spongy bone has the same matrix of collagen and mineral as compact bone.
Spongy bone is well supplied by the vessels of the marrow between its trabeculae.
Correct. More surface means faster turnover in either direction.

why.correct: In the proliferative zone, chondrocytes divide rapidly and line up in stacks. Their division supplies the cells whose later enlargement lengthens the bone.
options: The reserve zone has small, scattered cells that rarely divide, nearest the epiphysis.
In the zone of calcified matrix the chondrocytes are dead and the matrix is calcified.
Correct. Stacks of flat, dividing cells mark the proliferative zone.
In the zone of maturation and hypertrophy the cells have stopped dividing and are much larger.

why.correct: The reserve zone lies against the epiphysis. Its scattered chondrocytes rarely divide; the zone anchors the plate to the epiphysis.
options: The proliferative zone lies just below it, with cells in stacks.
Correct. The zone nearest the epiphysis is the reserve zone.
The zone of maturation and hypertrophy is farther toward the diaphysis, with enlarged cells.
The zone of calcified matrix is the last zone before bone, nearest the diaphysis.

why.correct: The primary ossification center forms in the diaphysis when a nutrient artery invades the calcified middle of the cartilage model and osteoblasts lay down spongy bone.
options: Secondary ossification centers form later, in the epiphyses.
The epiphyseal plate is the disc of cartilage left between epiphysis and diaphysis at the end of the process.
The medullary cavity opens later, when osteoclasts clear the spongy bone from the center.
Correct. The first bone in the shaft is the primary ossification center.

why.correct: The epiphyseal line is the thin line of bone left where an epiphyseal plate used to be, after growth in length has stopped.
options: An epiphyseal plate is cartilage in a growing bone. This bone is mature, and the plate has been replaced.
Correct. A plate that has closed leaves an epiphyseal line.
Articular cartilage covers the joint surface at the very end of the bone.
The metaphysis is the whole flared region; the pinned feature is the thin line within it.

why.correct: The flat bones of the skull roof form by intramembranous ossification: osteoblasts differentiate from mesenchymal cells within a sheet of mesenchyme and lay down bone directly, with no cartilage stage.
options: Cartilage models are the starting point for endochondral ossification, which forms the limb bones, vertebrae and skull base.
Fibrocartilage is not a template for bone formation.
Correct. Skull roof bones form directly in mesenchyme.
Epiphyseal plates are found in growing long bones, not in flat skull bones.

why.correct: The flat bones of the skull dome form directly in mesenchyme and grow at their edges, without cartilage models or epiphyseal plates. A defect in plate chondrocytes shortens the long bones, which lengthen at the plates, and spares bones that never use them.
options: Correct. No cartilage, no plates, so a plate defect cannot slow them.
The skull dome never has epiphyseal plates at all; they are features of long bones.
All bone, including skull bone, is laid down by osteoblasts.
The skull dome has no cartilage model to replace; that is the point of intramembranous ossification.

why.correct: Growth in length depends on the plate's cartilage continuing to divide and being replaced by bone. A bony bridge tethers the epiphysis to the diaphysis and stops growth at that site, so the leg can end up shorter, or angled if only one side is bridged.
options: Width comes from appositional growth at the periosteum, which a plate injury does not stop or speed.
Correct. A bridged plate cannot push the epiphysis away, so lengthening slows or stops.
The medullary cavity is carved and kept open by osteoclasts; the plate injury does not change that.
Articular cartilage is separate from the plate and stays cartilage for life.

why.correct: Growth in length starts with cell division in the proliferative zone. Block it and less cartilage is made, lengthening slows, and the plate thins because replacement by bone continues. Growth in width uses a different mechanism and continues.

variables.name: Number of new chondrocytes made in the plate
variables.why: The proliferative zone is where plate chondrocytes divide; blocking division stops new cells being made.

variables.name: Rate of growth in length
variables.why: Fewer new cells means less cartilage added to push the epiphysis away, so there is less cartilage for bone to replace and the diaphysis lengthens more slowly.

variables.name: Appositional growth at the periosteum
variables.why: Width growth depends on osteoblasts under the periosteum, which the drug does not target.

variables.name: Thickness of the epiphyseal plate
variables.why: Bone keeps replacing cartilage on the diaphysis side while little new cartilage is added on the epiphysis side, so the plate thins.

why.correct: A cartilage model forms first. Its middle calcifies and many of its chondrocytes die, while the perichondrium becomes periosteum and lays a bone collar. A nutrient artery brings in bone-forming cells, creating the primary ossification center; osteoclasts then hollow out the medullary cavity. Around birth and in childhood, the epiphyses ossify from secondary centers.

From the epiphysis: resting cells in the reserve zone, dividing cells in the proliferative zone, enlarging cells in the zone of maturation and hypertrophy, and dying cells in calcified matrix, which bone then replaces.

Intramembranous ossification has no cartilage stage: osteoblasts secrete osteoid directly in the mesenchyme. A cartilage model belongs to endochondral ossification, and chondrocytes, not osteoblasts, build it.
options: This step is right. An ossification center begins as clustered mesenchymal cells becoming osteoblasts.
This is the error. Osteoblasts secrete osteoid, not cartilage, and this route uses no cartilage model.
This step is right. Osteoid mineralizes, and enclosed osteoblasts become osteocytes.
This step is right. Spongy bone forms first, and surface mesenchyme becomes periosteum.
This step is right. Compact bone forms at the surfaces, with spongy bone between.

why.correct: Cartilage has no blood vessels, so chondrocytes depend on diffusion through their matrix. Calcified matrix blocks diffusion, many of the chondrocytes die, and their empty spaces are invaded by vessels and bone-forming cells.
options: Chondrocytes make cartilage matrix, not osteoid. Osteoid is laid down by osteoblasts, which arrive with the vessels.
Correct. Calcified matrix starves the chondrocytes.
Division into stacks happens in the proliferative zone of the plate, before cells enlarge, not after calcification.
Cartilage is not converted into bone. It is removed and replaced by bone laid down by osteoblasts.

why.correct: Those thin lines are epiphyseal lines. His plates have closed and been replaced by bone, so there is no cartilage left to grow interstitially. No supplement can add length. His bones can still thicken slowly by appositional growth.
options: Growth in length needs an open plate of cartilage. The lines show his plates have closed.
An epiphyseal line is bone, and bone cannot grow from within, so there is nothing to stimulate.
Correct. Closed plates mean no more growth in length.
Appositional growth at the periosteum continues through life, so width can still increase slowly.

why.correct: Cartilage does not harden into bone. Its matrix calcifies, many of its chondrocytes die, and invading osteoblasts lay bone on the leftover calcified columns, which osteoclasts later clear away. Bone replaces the cartilage.
options: The model is hyaline cartilage, and bone replaces it; it does not turn into another kind of cartilage.
Calcified cartilage is still cartilage; it only serves as a temporary scaffold for new bone.
Only the articular cartilage and, until growth ends, the epiphyseal plate remain. The rest is removed.
Correct. The model is a template that bone replaces.

why.correct: Appositional growth adds new bone under the periosteum, on the outside. Osteoclasts on the endosteum remove bone from the inside, widening the medullary cavity. The bone widens without its wall becoming ever thicker and heavier.
options: Correct. Build outside, remove inside.
There is no cartilage in the shaft wall to divide, and adding bone inside would narrow the cavity.
That reversal would make the bone narrower, not wider.
The epiphyseal plate adds length at the ends; it does not add bone to the shaft's surface.

why.correct: Interstitial growth needs a matrix that can stretch as cells inside it divide and add more matrix. Cartilage matrix can; mineralized bone matrix cannot. Bone can only grow by adding layers to a surface, so length is gained by growing cartilage that bone then replaces.
options: Bone is richly supplied with blood, through nutrient arteries and central canals.
Correct. Rigid matrix rules out growth from within.
Osteocytes do not divide at all, but even dividing cells could not expand rigid matrix around themselves.
Osteoblasts work on bone surfaces everywhere, including under the periosteum and endosteum.

why.correct: Appositional growth adds new layers to a surface. Bone grows wider this way, skull bones thicken this way, and cartilage can also grow this way from its perichondrium. Division and swelling of cells inside the plate expand the tissue from within: interstitial growth.
options: Correct. Adding bone to the outer surface is appositional.
Division inside the tissue is interstitial growth.
Correct. Layering bone onto a surface is appositional.
Swelling of cells inside the plate expands it from within: interstitial.
Correct. New cartilage laid on the surface by cells of the perichondrium is appositional.

why.correct: Bone growth needs removal as well as building. Osteoclasts hollow the medullary cavity, clear old cartilage below the plates and keep marrow spaces open. Without them, bone piles up: dense bone, a small cavity and little room for red marrow.

variables.name: Size of the medullary cavity
variables.why: Osteoclasts open and widen the medullary cavity. Without resorption, the cavity stays small and filled with bone.

variables.name: Density of the bones
variables.why: Osteoblasts keep adding bone and none is removed, so the bones become abnormally dense.

variables.name: Space available for red marrow
variables.why: Marrow lives in the medullary cavity and the spaces of spongy bone, which stay filled with bone when it is not cleared.

variables.name: Clearing of calcified cartilage below the epiphyseal plate
variables.why: Osteoclasts remove the old calcified cartilage and first bone below the plate; without them this material accumulates.

why.correct: Secondary ossification centers form in the epiphyses, around birth and through childhood, after the primary center has formed in the diaphysis.
options: Correct. The ends of the bone ossify from secondary centers.
The middle of the diaphysis is the site of the primary ossification center.
The periosteum lays down the bone collar and adds width; it is not an ossification center.
The medullary cavity is a space carved out by osteoclasts, not a site where bone forms.

why.correct: The fracture hematoma is the clotted blood that pools around a break from torn vessels in the periosteum, bone and marrow. It is the first stage of repair.
options: The external callus forms later, as cartilage and collagen bulging around the outside of the break.
Correct. Clotted blood filling the break is the fracture hematoma.
The bony callus of spongy bone forms weeks later, after the cartilage callus.
The fibrocartilaginous callus forms later, when capillaries, fibroblasts and chondrocytes turn the clot into collagen and cartilage.

why.correct: The external callus is the collar of fibrocartilage and collagen around the outside of the break. With the internal callus, it splints the broken ends.
options: Correct. The outer bulge of the soft callus is the external callus.
The periosteum is the thin membrane over the bone; the callus bulges well beyond it.
The hematoma is clotted blood, the stage before the callus forms.
The internal callus lies between the broken ends and in the medullary cavity, not around the outside.

why.correct: A greenstick fracture is incomplete: the bone breaks on one side and bends on the other, like a fresh twig. It is typical of children.
options: A transverse fracture goes straight across the whole bone.
In an impacted fracture, one end of a complete break is driven into the other.
Correct. A break partway across is a greenstick fracture.
A comminuted fracture breaks the bone into three or more pieces.

why.correct: A comminuted fracture shatters the bone into three or more fragments, usually from a high-energy injury or a fall on fragile bone.
options: A compression fracture crushes spongy bone, such as a vertebra. This shaft is broken into several pieces.
Correct. Several fragments make it comminuted.
An oblique fracture is a single break at an angle.
A greenstick fracture is a break only partway across.

why.correct: Both curves climb through childhood and the teens, level off, and reach their highest point at about 30 to 40 years before starting to fall.
options: At 10, both curves are still climbing steeply.
At 15 to 20, both curves are still rising.
Correct. The curves reach their plateau and peak at about 30 to 40.
By 55, both curves are falling, and the female curve is falling steeply.

why.correct: The female curve drops steeply between about 50 and 60, far faster than at any other time or in men. Those are the years around the end of a woman's reproductive life, when a hormonal brake on osteoclasts is lost.
options: Correct. The steepest drop on the graph is the female curve in the fifties.
Men are at or near their peak at 30 to 40; their curve is almost flat there.
Men do lose bone steadily late in life, but the slope is gentle compared with women in their fifties.
After 60, the female curve falls again at a gentle, steady rate, much like the male curve.

why.correct: Repair runs from hematoma to soft callus to bony callus to remodeling. The hematoma is invaded by vessels and becomes a soft callus of collagen and cartilage; that cartilage is replaced by spongy bone, as in endochondral ossification; and remodeling restores compact bone and the bone's shape over months to years.

Bone follows load. Without load, osteocytes shift their signals toward resorption: osteoclasts work harder, osteoblasts less, bone mass falls and calcium is released. Spongy bone, with its large surface, loses bone fastest.

variables.name: Load on the leg bones
variables.why: Lying in bed, the legs no longer carry body weight or the pull of walking muscles.

variables.name: Osteoclast activity
variables.why: Unloaded osteocytes release more of the signal that makes osteoclasts form, so resorption rises.

variables.name: Osteoblast activity
variables.why: Unloaded osteocytes release more of the signal that holds osteoblasts back, so formation falls.

variables.name: Bone mass
variables.why: With resorption above formation, each remodeling cycle removes more bone than it replaces: Wolff's law in reverse.

variables.name: Calcium released from the leg bones
variables.why: Osteoclasts dissolve mineral, so more calcium leaves the bones; much of it is lost in the urine.

why.correct: Wolff's law: bone adapts to the loads placed on it. Years of hitting loaded the racket arm's bones heavily, osteocytes signaled for more formation and less resorption, and bone was added until the thicker wall brought strain back down.
options: Both arms receive the same blood, so a difference between them cannot come from something carried in it.
Growth plates in the two arms close at about the same time, and thicker walls reflect width, not length.
Correct. Load drives bone formation.
Marrow type does not thicken the bone's wall, and adult upper arm shafts hold mainly yellow marrow.

why.correct: A fracture with broken skin over it is an open fracture. The wound lets bacteria reach the bone, so infection of the bone is the main added danger, which makes it an emergency.
options: A closed fracture has intact skin; this one has a wound.
A greenstick fracture is an incomplete break in a child's bone; a bone end through the skin is a complete break.
It may also be comminuted, but the defining feature described is the skin wound, and the main danger is infection.
Correct. Broken skin makes it open, and infection is the main extra risk.

why.correct: A twisting force applied along a long bone breaks it along a helix that winds around the shaft: a spiral fracture.
options: A transverse fracture runs straight across the bone and usually comes from a direct blow or bending, not twisting.
Correct. Twisting makes a spiral fracture.
An impacted fracture comes from a force driving one end into the other, along the bone's length.
A compression fracture crushes spongy bone, such as a vertebra, under a squeezing load.

why.correct: A child's bone has proportionally more collagen and less mineral than an adult's, so it is more flexible. Under a bending load it can crack on the stretched side and bend on the other, like a green twig.
options: Children's bones have compact bone walls, just thinner than adults'.
Correct. More flexible bone bends and breaks partway.
Growth plates are near the ends of the bone, not in the shaft where greenstick fractures occur.
Osteoclast numbers do not explain how a bone breaks in the moment of injury.

why.correct: Bone remodeling replaces old bone with new at the same site, resorption followed by formation, with little change in size or shape.
options: In bone modeling, building and removal happen on different surfaces, which changes the bone's shape or size.
Appositional growth adds layers to a surface and makes the bone wider.
Correct. Same site, old for new, no change in shape: remodeling.
Endochondral ossification replaces cartilage with bone during development, not old bone with new.

why.correct: Osteocytes do not divide or build new bone. Osteoblasts, made from osteogenic cells, move into the pit and fill it with osteoid over about three to four months.
options: This step is right. Osteocytes act as the sensors that start remodeling.
This step is right. Osteoclasts form by fusion of precursors from the blood.
This step is right. Resorption is the fast part of the cycle.
This is the error. Osteoblasts, not osteocytes, fill the pit, and osteocytes never divide.
This step is right. Osteoid laid by osteoblasts mineralizes over time.

why.correct: After the hematoma, capillaries, fibroblasts and chondrocytes turn it into a soft fibrocartilaginous callus, which bone then replaces.
options: An epiphyseal plate is the growth cartilage of a growing long bone, not a stage of repair.
Correct. The soft callus comes between hematoma and bony callus.
A primary ossification center is a stage of development before birth, not of fracture repair.
Granulation tissue does form in the hematoma, but the stage that follows is named for the callus of collagen and cartilage it produces.

why.correct: In osteoporosis, resorption has outpaced formation for years, so there is too little bone, with thin and disconnected trabeculae and a thinner compact wall. The bone that remains has normal mineral in its matrix.
options: Soft, poorly mineralized bone is a different disease, caused by too little vitamin D. In osteoporosis the mineral content of the remaining bone is normal.
Faulty collagen causes brittle bone disease from childhood, not the age-related loss of bone mass in osteoporosis.
Correct. Osteoporosis is a lack of bone, not a lack of mineral in the bone.
Trabeculae thin and disconnect in osteoporosis; they do not thicken.

why.correct: Anything that lowers peak bone mass or tips remodeling toward resorption raises the risk: long-term steroid medicines, smoking, a low peak and female sex (a lower peak and faster loss after the reproductive years).
options: Correct. Long-term steroid medicines slow bone formation.
Weight-bearing exercise loads bone and, through Wolff's law, protects it.
Correct. Smoking lowers bone mass and slows fracture healing.
Correct. A low peak leaves less bone to lose before it becomes fragile.
Correct. Women reach a lower peak and lose bone fast for several years at the end of their reproductive years.
Enough calcium and vitamin D supports bone formation and is part of prevention.

why.correct: Early healing depends on capillaries growing into the hematoma and a soft callus bridging the gap. Too much movement tears these fragile structures again and again, so the bony callus is delayed and the break may fail to join.
options: Load helps bone once the callus is firm, during remodeling. Early movement at the break itself disrupts the soft callus.
Correct. Motion keeps breaking the new vessels and callus.
More bleeding does not produce a stronger repair; it only adds swelling.
Remodeling to compact bone comes last and needs a stable bony callus first.

why.correct: The soft and bony calluses depend on new capillaries growing into the hematoma, bringing oxygen, nutrients and the cells that become fibroblasts, chondrocytes and osteoblasts. Poor blood supply slows that ingrowth, so every later stage is delayed.
options: Clotting does not depend on the vessels growing in; a clot forms in minutes either way.
Osteocyte death at the ends is caused by the injury itself, not by the patient's circulation.
Correct. The callus is built by cells that arrive with new vessels.
Remodeling is last and would be slow too, but the first bottleneck is the vessel ingrowth that the callus needs.

why.correct: Reduction means putting the broken ends back into line. When a surgeon does it through an incision, often with plates, screws or a rod, it is an open reduction.
options: Correct. Aligning the ends through a surgical opening is open reduction.
Closed reduction aligns the ends from outside without cutting the skin.
An open fracture is a type of break with a wound over it, not a treatment.
Bone modeling is a natural process of shaping bone, not a surgical procedure.

why.correct: Total blood calcium is held between about 8.5 and 10.5 mg/dL (about 2.1 to 2.6 mmol/L), and each person's level stays within a much narrower band inside that range.
options: That is about double the normal level; a calcium near 19 mg/dL would be a life-threatening hypercalcemia.
Correct. Normal total calcium is about 8.5 to 10.5 mg/dL.
Those numbers are the normal fasting range for glucose in the blood, not calcium.
Those numbers look like the normal range for blood sodium in mmol/L, not calcium.

why.correct: Tingling and a hand spasm with the cuff are signs of overexcitable nerves and muscles, the hallmark of hypocalcemia. A calcium of 6.8 mg/dL is well below the normal 8.5 to 10.5 mg/dL.
options: Correct. Low calcium makes nerves and muscles overexcitable.
9.6 mg/dL is in the middle of the normal range and would not cause tetany.
10.4 mg/dL is at the top of normal; it would not make nerves overexcitable.
13.5 mg/dL is hypercalcemia, which makes nerves and muscles less excitable: weakness, not spasm.

why.correct: Calcium ions on the outside of the membrane make voltage-gated sodium channels harder to open. With fewer of them, the channels open with little or no stimulus, so nerves and muscles fire spontaneously: tingling, cramps and tetany. Contraction itself still has enough calcium, mostly from stores inside muscle cells.
options: Muscle cells do not respond to low blood calcium by storing more inside. The effect is on the membrane's sodium channels.
Low calcium does not wipe out the resting potential. It changes how easily the sodium channels open.
Correct. Less calcium outside, less brake on the sodium channels, more firing.
Very low calcium can reduce neurotransmitter release, which would weaken signals. The dominant effect, overexcitability, comes from the sodium channels.

why.correct: Osteoclasts driven by the tumor release calcium from bone faster than the kidneys can excrete it, so he develops hypercalcemia. Extra calcium makes nerves and muscles less excitable (weakness, confusion) and stops the kidneys concentrating urine (thirst, large volumes of urine).
options: Tingling, spasm and a low calcium describe hypocalcemia, the opposite of what extra bone resorption causes.
Correct. Hypercalcemia with its typical less-excitable picture.
Tumor-driven osteoclasts release calcium independently of the feedback loop, so a normal calcium is unlikely.
12.0 mg/dL is high, but seizures and tetany are signs of low calcium; a high calcium dampens excitability.

why.correct: Low calcium triggers the calcium-raising hormone, which acts on all three effectors: bone releases calcium, the kidneys keep calcium and lose phosphate, and the kidneys activate vitamin D so the intestine absorbs more. Calcium rises, and hormone release falls again: negative feedback.

variables.name: Release of the calcium-raising hormone from the small glands behind the thyroid
variables.why: Fewer calcium ions bind the receptor protein on the gland cells, so they release more hormone within seconds.

variables.name: Osteoclast activity
variables.why: The hormone acts on osteoblasts, which signal more osteoclasts to form and work harder, releasing calcium from bone.

variables.name: Calcium lost in the urine
variables.why: The hormone makes the kidney tubules return more calcium from the forming urine to the blood.

variables.name: Phosphate lost in the urine
variables.why: The hormone makes the kidneys keep less phosphate, so more is excreted and it does not bind the freed calcium.

variables.name: Activation of vitamin D in the kidneys
variables.why: The hormone switches on the kidney step that finishes activating vitamin D.

variables.name: Calcium absorbed from food by the intestine
variables.why: More activated vitamin D makes the intestinal lining absorb more calcium, over a day or more.

why.correct: Vitamin D deficiency cuts calcium absorption. The loop defends blood calcium by raising the calcium-raising hormone, which takes calcium from bone and dumps phosphate in the urine. Blood calcium may stay near normal, but bone pays: resorption rises and new matrix cannot mineralize, which in children causes rickets.

variables.name: Fraction of dietary calcium absorbed by the intestine
variables.why: Without vitamin D to activate, the intestinal lining makes too few calcium transport proteins, so it absorbs only a small fraction of the calcium eaten.

variables.name: Release of the calcium-raising hormone
variables.why: Less calcium enters the blood, calcium dips, and the gland cells release more hormone to hold it up.

variables.name: Osteoclast activity
variables.why: More calcium-raising hormone acts through osteoblasts to drive osteoclasts, withdrawing calcium from bone.

variables.name: Phosphate lost in the urine
variables.why: The raised hormone makes the kidneys keep less phosphate.

variables.name: Mineralization of newly laid osteoid
variables.why: Too little calcium and phosphate reach new osteoid, so it stays soft and unmineralized.

why.correct: The gland cells are both sensor and control center: less calcium bound means more hormone. The hormone acts on bone and the kidneys quickly and, through activated vitamin D, on the intestine more slowly. As calcium rises, more binds the gland cells and hormone release falls, closing the negative feedback loop.
When calcium is low, the calcium-raising hormone makes the kidney tubules return more calcium to the blood, so less, not more, is lost in the urine. It is phosphate that the kidneys excrete more of.
options: This step is right. Low calcium increases the hormone's release.
This step is right. Bone resorption releases calcium into the blood.
This is the error. The kidneys keep more calcium when it is low; they excrete more phosphate.
This step is right. The hormone switches on the kidney step that activates vitamin D.
This step is right. Activated vitamin D increases calcium absorption.

why.correct: Activated vitamin D acts on the intestinal lining, which makes more calcium transport proteins and absorbs more of the calcium in food. Because it works through new proteins, this takes a day or more.
options: Laying down osteoid would take calcium out of the blood as it mineralizes, not raise blood calcium.
Correct. The intestine is vitamin D's main target in the loop.
Excreting more calcium would lower blood calcium.
Less hormone is the result once calcium has risen, not the step that raises it.

why.correct: Absorbed: 25% of 800 = 200 mg. Net from the gut: 200 − 100 = 100 mg. Out in urine: 150 mg. Output exceeds net input by 150 − 100 = 50 mg a day, and bone supplies that difference to keep the blood level steady.
options: She would be in balance only if net absorption equaled urine loss; here it is 100 mg against 150 mg.
Correct. 150 mg lost in urine minus 100 mg net absorbed leaves a 50 mg daily shortfall that bone covers.
100 mg is her net absorption from the gut, not the shortfall.
200 mg is the amount absorbed before the 100 mg released back into the gut is subtracted.

why.correct: The loop protects blood calcium first. When intake falls short, the calcium-raising hormone increases bone resorption and kidney calcium saving, so the blood level stays normal. By mass balance, the shortfall comes out of the skeleton, which slowly thins.
options: A normal blood level says the loop is working, not that intake is enough. The shortfall is being covered by bone.
Correct. Normal blood calcium, thinning bone.
The kidneys can keep calcium from being lost, but no organ can make calcium; it can only be absorbed from food.
A normal result is exactly what the loop is expected to produce, even with a poor intake.

why.correct: Calcium triggers contraction, triggers neurotransmitter exocytosis, is needed in clotting, forms bone mineral with phosphate, and, from outside the cell, sets how easily sodium channels open.
options: Correct. A rise in calcium inside muscle cells starts contraction.
Correct. Calcium entry into the nerve ending triggers neurotransmitter exocytosis.
Correct. Several clotting steps need calcium ions.
Oxygen is carried by an iron-containing protein in red blood cells, not by calcium.
Correct. Bone mineral is calcium phosphate.
Correct. Extracellular calcium acts as a brake on voltage-gated sodium channels.

why.correct: About half of plasma calcium is free Ca2+. That is the active form: it binds the gland cells' receptor protein, sets nerve and muscle excitability and takes part in clotting.
options: Protein-bound calcium, about 40%, is a reserve that trades with the free pool; it does not act directly.
Correct. Free ions are the regulated, active form.
Calcium bound to small ions is about 10% of the total and is not the form cells sense.
Red blood cells do not store calcium for the blood.

why.correct: The intestine absorbs calcium well only under the influence of activated vitamin D, and the last activation step happens in the kidneys. Failing kidneys cannot finish it, so absorption falls however much sun or vitamin D he gets.
options: Correct. No final kidney step, little activated vitamin D, poor absorption.
Nothing here raises absorption: failing kidneys make less activated vitamin D, and activated vitamin D is what drives the intestine to absorb calcium.
The skin makes vitamin D, but it stays inactive until the kidneys complete its activation, so absorption cannot hold steady.

why.correct: Bone resorption releases calcium and phosphate together, and phosphate binds calcium. Excreting the extra phosphate keeps it from binding the freed calcium, so the free calcium level can rise.
options: Phosphate in the urine does not pull calcium from the kidneys; the hormone is making the kidneys keep calcium at the same time.
Correct. Removing phosphate stops it from binding the calcium that bone releases.
Building more bone would take calcium out of the blood, the opposite of what the loop needs.
The gland cells' receptor protein binds calcium; phosphate excretion acts on the blood, not on that receptor protein.

why.correct: Activated vitamin D acts inside the intestinal cells to switch on the making of calcium channels, carriers and pumps. Making new proteins takes a day or more, so the intestine handles long-term balance while bone and the kidneys handle quick changes.
options: Existing osteoclasts respond to the calcium-raising hormone within hours, so bone is one of the fast effectors.
The kidneys filter the blood continuously, and their calcium handling changes within minutes to hours.
Correct. Activated vitamin D works by making new transport proteins, which takes a day or more.

why.correct: With no thyroid, she has none of its calcium-lowering hormone, yet her calcium is normal. The calcium-raising hormone from the small glands, with activated vitamin D, does the everyday regulation; when calcium rises, its release simply falls. Many exams still present the thyroid's calcium-lowering hormone as an equal partner, but its adult role is minor.
options: If it were the main regulator, losing it would disturb her calcium. It did not.
Her tablets replace the thyroid's other hormones, which set how fast cells use fuel, not the calcium-lowering hormone.
Correct. Normal calcium without it shows its adult role is small.
The small glands make the calcium-raising hormone, not the thyroid's calcium-lowering one.

why.correct: Teenagers need about 1,300 mg of calcium a day, vitamin D to absorb it, protein for the collagen matrix, and load on the bones: through Wolff's law, weight-bearing and impact exercise signals osteocytes to add bone. Peak bone mass built now protects her decades later.
options: Correct. 1,300 mg a day is the teen target.
Correct. Without vitamin D she absorbs little of what she eats.
Correct. Collagen is protein, and most of the organic matrix is collagen.
Swimming is excellent exercise, but the water carries her weight, so it loads bone far less than running or jumping.
Correct. Impact loading drives bone formation.
Soft drinks replacing milk remove a major calcium source and add none.

why.correct: The cells of the four small glands behind the thyroid carry a receptor protein that binds calcium, and they set their own hormone release in response. They sense and decide in the same cells.
options: Osteocytes sense mechanical load on bone, not the calcium level of the blood for this loop.
The kidney tubules are effectors: they change how much calcium is kept.
Correct. The gland cells are sensor and control center together.
The intestinal lining is an effector, acting on activated vitamin D's signal.
